name: Harava identification database
description: Harava's own rules for radios that Fieldwatch's signatures leave unidentified. Rules are tried in order; the first that matches wins. A rule only changes the layer of a radio that Fieldwatch did not identify; for the others it adds the 'Identified as' text. Company names come from bt_assigned_numbers.json (Bluetooth SIG).

match (all given conditions must hold).name_regex: regular expression on the advertised name (case-insensitive)
match (all given conditions must hold).mfg: Bluetooth company ID of the manufacturer data, 4 hex digits, e.g. 004C = Apple
match (all given conditions must hold).mfg_data_prefix: hex the manufacturer data (after the company ID) starts with
match (all given conditions must hold).ad_type: advertising data type in the raw advertisement, 2 hex digits, e.g. 2B = Mesh Beacon
match (all given conditions must hold).ad_data_prefix: hex the data of that AD structure starts with
match (all given conditions must hold).ad_data_regex: regular expression on the hex (upper case) of the data of that AD structure, for patterns a prefix cannot tell
match (all given conditions must hold).service_data_regex: regular expression on the hex of the Service Data of service_data_uuid
match (all given conditions must hold).service_data_uuid: 16-bit UUID of Service Data, 4 hex digits
match (all given conditions must hold).service_uuid_any: list of 16-bit service UUIDs; one of them must be advertised
match (all given conditions must hold).uuid128_any: list of 128-bit service UUIDs (8-4-4-4-12); one of them must be advertised

schema.group: how to tell that several rotating addresses are the same device: take bytes [from, to) of the AD structure ad_type, of the manufacturer data (source = mfg) or of the service data of uuid (source = service_data). key (optional) names the group; rules with the same key join the same devices, e.g. two kinds of advert from one Mesh device
schema.confidence: high = the protocol says so; medium = typical, well known; low = a likely guess
schema.name_from_group: a nameless address that belongs to a group whose other addresses tell a name is identified again with that name, so e.g. the nameless Mesh beacons of a "Charge" device also become EV charging points

rules.name: Philips Hue lamp
rules.note: Advertises Signify's Hue Bluetooth service (FE0F). Hue lamps keep it on even when they have no name or a room name.

rules.name: Signify (Philips / WiZ) lighting
rules.note: Advertises a Bluetooth service number registered to Signify, the maker of Philips Hue and WiZ lights.

rules.name: Signify (Philips / WiZ) lighting
rules.note: Manufacturer data of Signify Netherlands B.V. (company 060F), the maker of Philips Hue and WiZ lights.

rules.name: EV charging point (DEFA?)
rules.note: A Bluetooth Mesh device named "Charge" that is waiting to be set up. Seen in numbers around a shared EV charging system of a housing company (most likely DEFA chargers, which are configured over Bluetooth); they advertise all day like mains-powered equipment. The maker is not confirmed by a public source, hence the question mark.

rules.note: A Bluetooth Mesh device named "Charge" that is waiting to be set up. Seen in numbers around a shared EV charging system of a housing company (most likely DEFA chargers, which are configured over Bluetooth); they advertise all day like mains-powered equipment. The maker is not confirmed by a public source, hence the question mark.

rules.name: EV charging point (DEFA?)
rules.note: A Bluetooth Mesh device waiting to be set up, whose device UUID has the form of the charge points named "Charge" (eight random bytes, then 80 and seven zero bytes). It did not tell its name in this data; every device of this form whose name was heard later was a charge point. Another product built on the same radio module could look the same.

rules.name: EV charging point (DEFA?)
rules.note: A Bluetooth Mesh device waiting to be set up, whose device UUID has the form of the charge points named "Charge" (eight random bytes, then 80 and seven zero bytes). It did not tell its name in this data; every device of this form whose name was heard later was a charge point. Another product built on the same radio module could look the same.

rules.name: EcoFlow power station
rules.note: EcoFlow names its devices EF-<model><serial>, e.g. EF-R3P… for a River 3 Plus.

rules.name: Oras smart faucet or shower
rules.note: Oras (Finland) makes Bluetooth faucets and showers.

rules.name: Ensto thermostat (ECO16BT or ELTE6-BT)
rules.note: By name. Ensto's Bluetooth thermostats for floor and room heating tell their model and the end of their address as the name; they are set with Ensto's phone app. The address is fixed.

rules.name: Ensto EV charger
rules.note: By name: EVH and a serial number, the form Ensto's EV chargers use. They also send Ensto's company number and a service of their own.

rules.name: EV charger
rules.note: By name: EVSE (electric vehicle supply equipment) and a number. Several makers name their chargers this way; the maker is not told.

rules.name: OBD diagnostic dongle (plugged into a car)
rules.note: By name. A dongle in a car's diagnostic socket that a phone app talks to. It is in a car, and usually stays there.

rules.name: Teltonika vehicle tracker (fleet GPS unit)
rules.note: By name: the model (FMB, FMC, FMM ...), a serial number and _LE, the form Teltonika's fleet trackers use. It is wired into a vehicle by its owner or operator and reports the vehicle's position over the mobile network; it is on the Vehicle layer because it tells of a vehicle nearby, not of something tracking you.

rules.name: Stoneridge SE5000 tachograph (lorry or bus)
rules.note: By name. The SE5000 is a digital tachograph, the driving-time recorder of a lorry or a bus; newer ones have Bluetooth for the driver's app.

rules.name: VDO DTCO tachograph (lorry or bus)
rules.note: By name. DTCO is the digital tachograph of VDO (Continental), the driving-time recorder of a lorry or a bus; the newer ones have Bluetooth for the driver's app. Seen only by name, so the confidence is low.

rules.name: Shared e-scooter
rules.note: By name. Rental scooters of one fleet were seen to share a name like this, each with a fixed address of its own. The operator is not told.

rules.name: Polestar car
rules.note: By name: the car advertises its model for the phone-as-key.

rules.name: Volvo car
rules.note: By name: the model name alone (EX90 ...) or VOLVO and a number. A guess from the name.

rules.name: S3XY buttons or light strip (Tesla accessory)
rules.note: By name. An accessory fitted inside a Tesla.

rules.name: Driversnote mileage beacon (in a car)
rules.note: By name. A small beacon kept in a car so that a mileage-log app on the driver's phone knows when a trip starts.

rules.name: Saphe traffic alarm (in a car)
rules.note: By name. A small box on a car's dashboard that warns of speed cameras and hazards through the driver's phone.

rules.name: Nut tracker tag
rules.note: By name. Nut key finders advertise the name nut. A tag of this kind has no finding network of its own like Apple's or Google's: it only rings and reports through its owner's phone app.

rules.name: SumUp card reader
rules.note: By name. A payment terminal of a shop, a market stall or a taxi.

rules.name: SwipBox parcel locker
rules.note: By name. A parcel locker without a screen: its doors are opened over Bluetooth from the carrier's phone app. It stands in one place.

rules.name: Sierzega traffic radar or speed display
rules.note: By name. Sierzega makes roadside radar units that count traffic and show drivers their speed; they are read out over Bluetooth.

rules.name: Brother label or mobile printer
rules.note: By name: a Brother model number and the end of the serial number.

rules.name: Epson printer
rules.note: By name: an Epson model series.

rules.name: ResMed sleep apnoea machine (CPAP)
rules.note: By name. A bedside breathing machine; it tells of a bedroom, and of its user's health, so mind where you publish it.

rules.name: Wilo heating pump
rules.note: By name: a circulation pump in a building's heating room.

rules.name: Grundfos pump
rules.note: By name: a circulation or water pump, usually in a building's heating room, set up with a phone app.

rules.name: Mitsubishi Electric air-conditioner adapter
rules.note: By name: the wireless adapter of an air conditioner or heat pump. Not a car.

rules.name: Gree air conditioner
rules.note: By name: an air conditioner or heat pump by Gree, also sold under other brands.

rules.name: Adjustable bed (motor control)
rules.note: By name: the motor control of an adjustable bed, used with a phone app.

rules.name: Pindora smart lock
rules.note: By name. A Bluetooth door lock or key box that is opened with a phone.

rules.name: Oclean electric toothbrush
rules.note: By name.

rules.name: IPSTube desk clock
rules.note: By name: a desk clock with small displays in place of nixie tubes.

rules.name: iPhone linked to a Windows PC (Phone Link?)
rules.note: Apple manufacturer data together with the 128-bit service 3E1D50CD-7E3E-427D-8E1C-B78AA87FE624, which Windows PCs advertise. So this is an Apple device that sends a Windows service: most likely an iPhone that is linked to a PC with Microsoft's Phone Link. Inferred from what was heard; the service is not documented. These radios tell the name "4".

rules.name: Windows PC
rules.note: Advertises the 128-bit service 3E1D50CD-7E3E-427D-8E1C-B78AA87FE624. Every radio with this service that told a name had a Windows PC name, apart from Apple devices that send it too (probably iPhones linked to a PC; they have a rule of their own before this one). So it is a Windows service shared by many PCs, not a fingerprint of one PC. Its public meaning is not documented.

rules.name: Bluetooth Mesh device, not set up
rules.note: An Unprovisioned Device Beacon: a smart lamp, plug or switch waiting to be added to a Bluetooth Mesh network. It changes its address often but keeps the same device UUID, so Harava can tell the addresses of one device apart from the others.

rules.name: Bluetooth Mesh network node
rules.note: A Secure Network Beacon of a set-up Bluetooth Mesh network (smart lighting and the like). The group is the network, not one device.

rules.name: Bluetooth Mesh device, not set up
rules.note: Mesh Provisioning service (1827): a device waiting to be added to a Bluetooth Mesh network, offering a phone a connection for the setup. Its service data carries the same device UUID as its Unprovisioned Device Beacons, so Harava joins both kinds of advert into one device.

rules.name: Bluetooth Mesh device, set up
rules.note: Mesh Proxy service (1828): a device that is already in a Bluetooth Mesh network and lets a phone connect to it.

rules.name: LE Audio device (earbuds, headphones or hearing aid)
rules.note: Bluetooth LE Audio services (audio stream control, broadcast scan, volume, microphone, hearing access …).

rules.name: AirPods or Beats
rules.note: Apple Proximity Pairing message.

rules.name: iPhone, iPad, Mac or Apple Watch
rules.note: Apple Nearby Info message, sent all the time by Apple devices.

rules.name: Apple device (Nearby Action: setup or Wi-Fi sharing)
Apple TV, HomePod or AirPlay speaker
Apple device looking for a hotspot
iBeacon (beacon of any maker)
rules.note: The iBeacon frame: Apple's company number, then 02 15, a 16-byte UUID, two numbers and the calibrated power. Apple defined the format and anyone may send it, so the company number says nothing about the maker: shop and museum beacons, door readers and some cars (Tesla) use it. When Fieldwatch has a signature for the UUID, the Signatures column tells whose it is.
rules.company: (iBeacon format: the maker is not told)

rules.name: Apple device
rules.note: An Apple message type that Harava does not know yet (for example 0x16 or 0x1C); most such messages come from iPhones, iPads and Macs.

rules.name: Samsung Galaxy device (phone, tablet, PC or watch)
rules.note: Samsung's 0x42 message, sent by Galaxy devices for SmartThings and nearby sharing.

rules.name: Windows device
rules.note: Microsoft manufacturer data (Swift Pair / connected devices).

rules.name: Oral-B electric toothbrush
rules.note: Company ID 0x00DC is Procter & Gamble, the owner of Oral-B; their Bluetooth toothbrushes advertise with it.

rules.name: BEHA heater
rules.note: Seen with the text 'Beha heater' in its manufacturer data.

rules.name: Ensto EV charger
rules.note: Ensto's company number together with the service UUID that its EV chargers advertise for the installer's and owner's app.

rules.name: Ensto thermostat (ECO16BT)
rules.note: Manufacturer data that begins with the text ECO16: the thermostat writes its model there. The company number in front of it reads 0x2806, Ensto's 0x0628 with its two bytes the other way round.

rules.name: Casambi lighting (lamp, sensor or switch)
rules.note: Casambi's company number. Casambi is a Bluetooth lighting-control system built into the lamps, sensors and switches of many makers; the name tells the product.

rules.name: Casambi lighting (lamp, sensor or switch)
rules.note: By name, for radios whose advertisement was not stored (a Sit export). Nearly every radio with a name of this form carried Casambi's company number: lamps and sensors of a building's lighting control.

rules.name: Bluetooth serial module (HM-10 type)
rules.note: Manufacturer data that begins with the letters HM followed by the module's own address, and the service FFE0: the stock firmware of the HM-10 family of serial modules. Such a module is a building block; what it is built into, the name may tell (a car diagnostic dongle, a hobby project, a tool).

rules.name: Google / Android device (service FEF3)
rules.note: Service data with Google's member UUID FEF3, in the form 4A 17 23 + four characters + 11. Google does not document it; most such advertisers are Android phones, watches and Google devices. In the data Harava was built on, the four characters behave like a code of one device that lasts about a day: the address changes every few minutes and the rest of the advertisement changes too, but the code stays, and no two advertisements with one code were ever heard at the same moment. Harava therefore shows the addresses with one code as one device. This is an observation, not a published fact.

rules.name: Google / Android device (service FEF3)
rules.note: Service data with Google's member UUID FEF3. Google does not document it; most such advertisers are Android phones and Google devices nearby, changing their address every few minutes. The advertisement itself stays the same over several address changes, so Harava shows the addresses that send the same one as one device.

rules.name: Google / Android device (service FCF1)
rules.note: Service data with Google's member UUID FCF1 (registered 2022). Not documented; seen from Android phones and watches. The address changes about every nine minutes, but the advertisement often stays the same over several changes (from minutes to hours), so Harava shows the addresses that send the same one as one device. One device can send two such advertisements at a time; they then appear as two devices that change address at the same moment.
